This sounds like it could be trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.

What to do now:
- Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
- Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
- Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
- Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.

Don't:
- Holding them tightly or covering their face.
- Offering food or water.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

This sounds like it could be bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.

The symptoms include:

- Swollen, tight belly
- Retching or trying to vomit with nothing coming up
- Restless, pacing, can't get comfortable
- Drooling, pale gums, collapse

What to do now:

- Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
- Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.

Don't:

- Waiting to see if it passes
- Giving food, water or home remedies
- Trying to make them vomit

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Yes, treat this as an emergency. For cats, every part of true lilies and daylilies is poisonous, including the pollen and the vase water. Even a small amount licked off the fur can cause deadly kidney failure. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Early treatment makes a big difference. Waiting 18 hours or more often leads to kidney damage that can't be reversed.

Before you go:
- Wipe the pollen off her fur with a damp cloth so she can't lick more.
- Bring the flower or a photo so the vet can identify it.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to.

She may look fine at first. Early signs include drooling, vomiting, low energy and not eating. Keep lilies out of homes with cats.

Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

All pets should be regularly vaccinated against rabies. Typically the first shot is done at a few months old, and additional shots are done every 1 or 3 years thereafter; your vet should track this and remind you when shots are due for each pet. Depending on where you live, doing this may be required by law, but even if not, it’s still a good idea. (There are also other vaccinations you should consider, but they vary by species.) Human vaccination is much less common. The idea is that if you get bitten by an animal not known to be vaccinated, then you will tell a doctor immediately and get the necessary shots. However, if you live in a country where rabies is endemic, then you should have a rabies vaccination before traveling abroad.

"Icky" or "tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

I actually run an animal rescue and take in kittens regularly. Kittens will need to eat more often than adult cats. If you don't feed them and ignore them, you'll be doing yourself and them more harm than good.

I'd suggest feeding them a moist food (like canned food) in the morning as the first meal of the day and dry food in the middle of the day. Then a moist food as the last meal of the day, if at all possible.

Typically a mother cat will nurse kittens every 2 hours. As they wean off the mother, they are still used to feeding often during the day. As already mentioned above, kittens need space to roam around and play.

The best solution to your problem is to get a good scratching post for your cats.

If you get a scratching post for your cats, they likely will not use your sofa at all to sharpen their claws.

A god scratching post needs to be heavy so your cat is not able to move it. This means it must weigh 15-20 kilos or more. The scratching surface must be made of sisal or hemp rope so your cat can use its full strength when scratching.

One single cat claw can hold the cat's weight, so they are strong.

For your cats sitting on the sofa, you can use a folded towel for them to lie/sit on.

It could also be his way of broadcasting his presence to any potential intruder or his dog-friends in the neighborhood. His way of saying "Here I am."

Q: Overweight lazy cat won't play Two months ago I took in my grandmother's cat after she passed away. He's a 13 year old tomcat who has been rather spoiled - my grandmother would feed him by hand - often 'luxury' … A: Seeing as your cat isn't into traditional cat toys, you might consider an interactive feeding toy. This has the benefit of forcing the cat to work for his food, this will both cut down on eating out of boredom and also motivate the cat to exercise/play to get fed. Here are some options which may work well for you: - Fill a small Kong with your cat's regular food (if it's dry food you can seal the top with some canned tuna to keep the kibble from falling out). - For dry food only use a more open feeder like this one: Catch Interactive Cat Feeder. Your cat has to work to move the food around with the help of a little bit of friction.

Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

This sounds like it could be bleeding & wounds. Most bleeding stops with firm, steady pressure. Bite wounds can look small but often get infected.

What to do now:
- If they're in pain, use a soft muzzle or towel so they don't bite. Skip this if they're vomiting or struggling to breathe.
- Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze for at least 5 minutes. Don't lift it to check.
- If blood soaks through, add more layers on top. Don't remove the first one.
- Once it stops, wrap it snugly but not tight. You should fit two fingers under the bandage.
- Go to the vet for anything deeper than a scrape, all bite wounds, and any bleeding that won't stop.

Don't:
- Tourniquets, unless you're trained. They can kill the limb.
- Hydrogen peroxide or alcohol in the wound. They damage tissue.
- Pulling out something stuck in the wound.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

This sounds like it could be vomiting & diarrhea. One episode in a bright, adult pet is often minor. Call your vet for advice and watch closely for the warning signs below.

Go to the vet now if:
- There's repeated vomiting, or they can't keep water down;
- Blood in the vomit or stool, or black, tarry stool;
- Swollen or painful belly, weakness or collapse;
- A puppy or kitten, or an unvaccinated young dog (parvovirus risk);
- May have swallowed a toy, bone or poison

What to do now:
- Call your vet and describe what you've seen. A photo helps.
- Offer small amounts of water often.
- If your vet agrees, feed small portions of bland food, like plain boiled chicken and rice for dogs.
- Keep a sick puppy away from other dogs and disinfect the area. Parvovirus spreads easily.

Don't:
- Human anti-diarrhea or stomach medicines. Some are toxic to cats and some dogs.
- Withholding food from a cat for more than a day. It can cause liver disease.

Call your vet for advice, and go in if it gets worse.

This is an emergency. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) can kill cats, and cats are far more sensitive to it than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Don't wait for signs.

Signs can start within a few hours:
- Brown or muddy-coloured gums
- Fast or deep breathing, weakness
- Swelling of the face or paws
- Vomiting, or yellow eyes and gums

Before you go:
- Bring the medicine pack and note when it happened and how many tablets may be missing.
- Only make her vomit if a vet tells you to, and don't give milk, food or any other medicine.

On the way, keep her calm in a carrier with good airflow. Keep all medicines where pets can't reach them.

Yes, this sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10â€“15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 Â°C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leaving a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat. Wet the coat and keep air moving instead.
- Waiting to see if they recover on their own.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Itching is a sign, not a disease. The three main causes are parasites (mainly fleas and mites, which are checked first), skin infections from bacteria, yeast or fungus, and allergies to things like insect bites, food, pollen, mold or dust. Itching only in certain seasons often points to a seasonal allergen.

Itching all year can point to dust mites or food. What to check at home:

- Look through the coat for fleas or flea dirt, and at the skin for redness, scabs or hair loss

Note where he scratches. Licking and rubbing of the feet and face is common with allergies and infections

See your vet if the itching lasts more than a few days, or if there is hair loss, scaling, a bad smell, or fluid on the skin. Please don't give human allergy pills or leftover steroids. Antihistamines often don't help dogs with allergies.

Manual removal is best, because it also allows you to clean/disinfect the wounds with isopropyl alcohol (or other disinfectant).

If she doesn't sit still for you to remove all of the ticks at once, you can try just pulling off one or two at a time, then giving her a break (petting her, giving her treats, playing a game, etc) before pulling off another tick or two. You can use some sprays or medications (many of them are found in these charts), but they can be dangerous if the dog is exposed to them multiple times in a single month. For example, if you treat her and then tomorrow your neighbor treats her because your neighbor didn't want to take care of her after the treatment, you might get bitten by a tick that came back into your home.

Act right away, even if the dog looks healthy.

- Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes
- Don't put garlic or other home remedies on it, and don't rely on "tandok" or "tambal" healers
- Go to the nearest Animal Bite Treatment Center (ABTC) or Animal Bite Center promptly for post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)
- Finish the full vaccine schedule the health workers give you

Don't wait for symptoms. Once rabies symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal. If the dog has an owner, they should report the bite and have the dog observed for 14 days.

The dog will not recognize a so-called silent treatment as a request to remedy its own behavior; it will never happen. Huskies, especially at that age, can be very problematic when it comes to being generally destructive. A friend of mine once had one at that age with separation anxiety, a common trait to Huskies. The dog completely destroyed the inside cab of his truck, chewing it completely down to the metal on the doors, the dash, and the seats trying to get out. The dog was left in the car for less than 30 minutes. Your dog will not associate distance or detachment the same way you do. You should actually be spending more time and effort observing your dog's behavior rather than waiting for signs of distress.

Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Executive Order No. 84 (1999) also calls for mass dog vaccination with free vaccines every March, Rabies Awareness Month.

Schedules differ by place, so watch for announcements from your barangay or ask your city or municipal veterinary office about the next free vaccination drive.

Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.
